brands.nikon: Nikon writes the shutter count into every photo's metadata, unencrypted. Use an unedited original file for best results.
brands.canon: Canon never writes the shutter count into image files — it is stored only inside the camera and read by service tools or USB utilities.
brands.sony: Sony stores the shutter count in an encrypted section of its metadata that cannot be decoded in the browser. Dedicated desktop utilities can read it over USB.
brands.fujifilm: Fujifilm bodies do not record a true shutter count, but some write a frame counter that gives a rough lower bound.
brands.pentax: Pentax obfuscates its shutter count field with a cipher, so it cannot be reliably read from files.
brands.olympus: OM System / Olympus bodies keep the full shutter count in an internal service menu; files sometimes carry a frame counter that hints at usage.
brands.panasonic: Panasonic does not write a shutter count to files. The service menu on the camera reports it.
brands.leica: Leica bodies generally do not store a shutter count in image files.

source.shutterCount: Read from the camera's shutter count metadata — this is the actual mechanical actuation counter.
source.mechanicalShutterCount: Read from the mechanical shutter counter — electronic-shutter frames are not included.
source.imageNumber: Estimated from the file's image number. This is a rough lower bound, not an exact actuation count — the counter can reset or roll over.

what-is-shutter-count.question: What is a shutter count?
what-is-shutter-count.answer: Shutter count is the number of times a camera's mechanical shutter has fired — the camera equivalent of a car's mileage. It is the most-checked indicator of wear when buying or selling a used camera, because shutters are rated for a finite number of actuations.

how-many-actuations-is-too-many.question: How many shutter actuations is too many?
how-many-actuations-is-too-many.answer: It depends on the camera class. Entry-level shutters are rated around 100,000 actuations, enthusiast bodies 150,000–200,000, and professional bodies 300,000–500,000. A rating is an average lifespan, not a hard limit — many shutters last far beyond it, and a low count on a poorly treated body can still mean problems.

why-no-canon-sony-shutter-count.question: Why can't I check the shutter count on my Canon or Sony photo?
why-no-canon-sony-shutter-count.answer: Canon never writes the shutter count into image files at all — it lives only in the camera's internal memory. Sony writes it, but encrypts that section of the metadata. In both cases a browser tool cannot read it from a photo; desktop utilities that connect to the camera over USB are the usual workaround.
